structure.title: The case for union
structure.text: Early essays argue against fragmentation and examine the weakness of the existing confederation.

structure.title: Defending the proposed machinery
structure.text: Later essays address representation, separate branches, federal powers, courts, and objections to the Constitution. Each belongs to a persuasion campaign.

people.name: Faction
people.text: A group pursuing interests potentially adverse to others' rights.

context.title: Ratification debate
context.text: These essays advocate adoption of a proposed constitution. They defend a design before readers know how it will function over generations.
context.takeaway: Treat predictions as arguments to evaluate.

context.title: Checking power
context.text: Different institutions receive distinct powers and incentives. The design attempts to use conflict to restrain domination rather than relying entirely on virtue.
context.takeaway: Ask what motivates the proposed check.

notice.text: Compare the language of safety with liberty.
notice.why: Strong government is defended as both a protection and a risk to manage.
The answer becomes clearer when its objection is reconstructed.

opening: The revolution has succeeded, and the new American union may still fail. Hamilton, Madison, and Jay must persuade readers to accept a stronger government without dismissing the fear that strong governments abuse their power. Their essays work through representation, faction, courts, and rival institutions, treating ambition as something a constitution must expect. The interest lies in watching political ideals become machinery: rules intended to keep people with competing interests governing together even when virtue is in short supply and nobody wants to lose.
